A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Navigation World Models and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Appendix sections and tables can be matched despite renumbering and substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-prediction, navigation-planning, trajectory-ranking, and ablation results, including additional datasets and visualizations in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds measured inference runtimes and Go Stanford adaptation and ablation results in Tables 8–9. The quantization runtime is explicitly an estimate.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the specified action encoder from summing embeddings of width d to concatenating three coordinate embeddings of width d/3 before adding temporal embeddings. Section 8.2 adds time-skipped and distilled inference and fine-tuning for adaptation. The CDiT backbone and CEM planning framework remain.

E1.justification: Both versions cover SCAND, TartanDrive, RECON, HuRoN, Ego4D, Go Stanford, and the same unfamiliar-image examples. Navigation and future-frame prediction remain the tasks. The new timing and adaptation studies change procedures within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: Table 9 expands the Go Stanford comparison with CDiT-L, reduced-context, action-only, two-goal, and adapted NWM variants. The original comparisons involving DIAMOND, DiT, GNM, NoMaD, and Forward are retained.

E3.justification: Original splits, metrics, and evaluation sets of 100 navigation examples and 500 prediction examples remain. New Section 8.2 measures single four-second trajectory runtimes, compares 16 versus 8 predicted states and 250 versus 6 denoising steps, and introduces 2,000-step adaptation. These are additional protocols, without evidence that original benchmarks were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds runtime analyses of time skipping and distillation, plus Go Stanford checks of model size, context, conditioning, goal count, and adaptation in Tables 8–9. Earlier architecture ablations, unlabeled-data analyses, navigation constraints, and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five post-training samples for mean/std reporting and three stochastic simulations for planning scores. v2 introduces no new seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance procedures. Table 9 supplies point estimates without additional uncertainty information.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values remain unchanged after matching appendix Tables 5/6/7 in v1 to Tables 7/5/6 in v2. New Table 8 reports runtimes of 30.3 seconds, 14.7 with time skipping, and 0.4 with additional distillation; 0.1 seconds with quantization is estimated. Table 9 adds ablation results and adapted LPIPS of 0.650 versus 0.652 without adaptation.

T1.justification: Equation 2 changes the action-aggregation endpoint from tau+k to tau+k-1. Equations 4–5 revise the planning action horizon and constraint-summation limits from T to T-1. These are limited formal revisions; the attention-complexity argument remains unchanged.

C1.justification: v1 attributes state-of-the-art performance to combining NWM with external policies; v2 attributes it to standalone NWM and describes the combination as competitive. Section 4.4 also narrows the ranking claim to improved navigation performance. The abstract and central contributions remain.

C2.justification: The new Discussion acknowledges uncertainty about NWM's learned representations and proposes possible emergence of allocentric representations. Section 8.2 adds interpretations about real-time feasibility and adaptation complementing planning. Existing limitations concerning mode collapse, pedestrian motion, and three-degree-of-freedom navigation remain.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents covariance prediction and variational-bound supervision, previously covered only indirectly through DiT defaults. Section 8.2 adds RTX 6000 Ada hardware, denoising-step counts, a FastVideo implementation reference, and adaptation-step information. Existing training, dataset, and planning details remain.

R1.justification: Six additional references support improved diffusion training, GPTQ quantization, phased consistency models, traversability/test-time adaptation, and egocentric-to-allocentric representations. The broader positioning relative to visual navigation, world models, and novel-view synthesis remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Limited rewrites clarify the formulation and diffusion description, condense constrained planning, and replace Conclusion with Discussion. Appendices A/B become Sections 7/8; citation style, acknowledgments, and an author affiliation change. Most prose and section order are retained.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-column report format with a two-column layout for the main text, references, and appendix text. It rebuilds the title page, places Figure 1 above the abstract, and resizes or relocates existing displays. Appendix tables are reordered, and Tables 8–9 are added.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful runtime and adaptation evidence absent from v1 and clarifies diffusion documentation and performance claims. These provide a limited gain in clarity and practical assessability while retaining the original benchmark evidence. The gains are bounded: Table 8 measures one trajectory and includes estimated quantization, while Table 9 lacks uncertainty and clearly specified adaptation/evaluation separation.
